analysis.one_liner: Bans small high-powered magnet sets sold for entertainment or stress relief to prevent child ingestion injuries.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on June 23, 2022 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would classify small, powerful magnet sets sold as toys, puzzles, jewelry, or stress-relief products as banned hazardous products under consumer product safety law. These magnets can be swallowed; when two or more are ingested, their magnetic force can pinch or twist sections of the intestines, causing serious injury or death. The bill also directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set safety standards for other small high-powered magnets within a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, teens, and families who would be protected from swallowing dangerous magnets. Congress's own findings state that ingesting two or more such magnets carries a high risk of abdominal catastrophe and death, often requiring high-cost medical intervention.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits small, high-powered magnets marketed for entertainment, jewelry, mental stimulation, stress relief, or combinations of those uses, effective 90 days after enactment, regardless of manufacture date.

The bill's findings document that when two or more high-powered magnets are swallowed, they can connect across different segments of body tissue, causing perforations, abscesses, bowel necrosis, and death, and that children almost universally require high-cost medical intervention after such ingestions.

Directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission to decide within three months whether a safety standard is needed for weaker-but-still-powerful magnets (flux index between 20 and 50 kG²mm²) and to issue a final standard within 12 months if needed.
Congress's findings state that evidence does not exist that warning labels alone would sufficiently reduce the hazard, which is why the bill bans the products rather than relying on warnings.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and sellers of high-powered magnet sets marketed for adults — such as magnetic puzzle and sculpture products — would lose the ability to sell those products in the U.S. market. Adult hobbyists who enjoyed the products would lose access to them.

drawbacks.text: The ban covers products regardless of the date of manufacture, meaning sellers could not clear out existing inventory, an immediate loss for retailers and importers of these magnet sets.

The ban applies to all such magnets even if sold with warnings or in age-restricted packaging; an honest supporter would acknowledge that adult collectors lose access to a legal product category entirely, based on risks to children who get hold of them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a narrow product category whose ingestion hazard, per the record, causes severe and sometimes fatal injuries to children who require costly emergency surgery. The cost is borne mainly by a small group of magnet-set manufacturers and by adults who lose access to a recreational product. The public health benefit plausibly outweighs the commercial cost, though a complete ban is a blunt instrument compared to age restrictions or packaging requirements.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, which killed it.

narrative.text: Rep. Tony Cárdenas (D-CA) introduced the Magnet Injury Prevention Act in the House on June 23, 2022, with Rep. Kim Schrier (D-WA) as a cosponsor.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day and received no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Bills referred to committee that receive no further action die automatically when the Congress ends; the bill would have to be reintroduced from scratch in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and retailers of high-powered magnet sets are better off because the bill never advanced — the products they sell remain legal and no restrictions were imposed. The Commission also remains free of the mandated rulemaking deadlines. Children retain the same exposure risk the bill sought to remove.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Magnet toy makers, since the bill never advanced

for.name: Rep. Tony Cárdenas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Magnet Injury Prevention Act on June 23, 2022, citing ingestion injuries and deaths from small high-powered magnets.

for.name: Rep. Kim Schrier
for.role: U.S. Representative (WA-8), cosponsor; a pediatrician by profession
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only member besides the sponsor to support it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsor and cosponsor were Democrats and no Republican took a recorded position; the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split can be measured. No opposition is documented in the record — it simply stalled.

industries.industry: High-powered magnet set manufacturers and sellers (e.g., magnetic puzzle and desk-toy makers)
industries.note: The bill would have banned their core products in the U.S. market within 90 days, covering existing inventory regardless of manufacture date. The products' hazard is the ingestion risk to children, so the industry's commercial interest runs against the safety benefit.
